newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin recovering, faces more Kremlin infighting.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin recovering, faces more Kremlin infighting.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, said by doctors to be in satisfactory shape 10 days after heart surgery, was boosted on Friday by a decision by Japan to release $500 million in aid to Russia but faced a new political scandal.

In their regular health bulletin on the 65-year-old president, published by the Kremlin press office, his doctors said Yeltsin's condition was "completely satisfactory" and that he had spent three hours working on official papers on Friday.
He has a steady pulse of 70 to 82 beats a minute and normal temperature and blood pressure, they said.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin's aides were preparing him for his first nationwide address after a quintuple bypass operation on November 5.
"All indicators are stable. His movements are being expanded," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

Yastrzhembsky announced on Tuesday that Yeltsin would make his address to the nation within days. He told Friday's briefing that aides were still deciding when the speech should be broadcast, either on television or radio.
"You understand, the imagemakers want the president's appearance to have a big impact," he said.
Doctors and Kremlin aides have been portraying the 65-year-old president as itching to get back to work to show he is well enough to serve out his four-year term, due to end in the year 2000.
Yeltsin is anxious to reassert control in the Kremlin to tackle growing economic problems and end months of infighting which has undermined his authority.
The economy got a shot in the arm from Japan's announcement that it would release $500 million in aid to Russia after Moscow offered to allow joint development of some disputed islands.
The dispute over the four islands, seized by the Soviet Union just before the end of World War Two, has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty.

In another significant move on the economy, an International Monetary Fund mission began talks with the government on whether to release the latest tranche of a $10 billion loan, held back because of Russia's poor tax collection.
Yeltsin was also lifted by the United States' decision to release an ex-KGB agent arrested on espionage charges. Moscow had threatened retaliatory measures if the case went ahead.
But Yeltsin faced new political intrigue in Moscow which could herald the start of more infighting.

A Russian newspaper published what it said was the transcript of a conversation last June between Viktor Ilyushin, then Yeltsin's top aide, and Anatoly Chubais, then part of Yeltsin's election campaign team and now Kremlin chief-of-staff.

The two men discussed the detention for several hours of two campaign aides which Chubais described as a provocation by Alexander Korzhakov, Yeltsin's personal security chief at the time. The showdown culminated in Korzhakov's dismissal.
The transcript suggested wrongdoings in the financing of Yeltsin's campaign for re-election.
Chubais said the conversation never took place and hinted that Korzhakov was behind the transcript.
"This is part of a campaign to discredit presidential authority after Boris Yeltsin's successful operation," Chubais told Interfax news agency.

Moskovsky Komsomolets said it had obtained the transcript from a security service. It published it hours before Korzhakov was due to register as a candidate in a local by-election, a move which could result in him gaining parliamentary immunity.

Russia's State Duma (lower house of parliament), which is packed with Chubais's enemies, passed a resolution calling on Yeltsin to state his position on the affair, which it linked to "criminalisation of the state".
Yastrzhembsky said he did not know Yeltsin's reaction to the transcript but confirmed the president was worried by intrigues around Korzhakov, who has turned against his former boss.
"I don't know about the president's immediate reaction to this publication. But generally he is very upset about what is happening around his former personal security chief," Yastrzhembsky said.
